meta.title: Who really said "'Dog Bites a Man' Is Not News. 'Man Bites a Dog' Is News"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Charles A. Dana was first credited with the man-bites-dog definition of news in 1902, after his 1897 death. Versions from 1899 name no one.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said ''Dog Bites a Man' Is Not News. 'Man Bites a Dog' Is News'?
meta.ogDescription: Not documented to Charles A. Dana. The saying was in print anonymously by 1899 and first pinned on Dana in 1902, after his death in 1897.

answer.label: Not documented to Charles A. Dana — an anonymous newsroom saying
answer.authorDates: In print by 1899 · first credited to Dana in 1902
answer.sourceLine: The line appears by 1899 with no author named: a fictional old reporter says it in Jesse Lynch Williams’s The Stolen Story and Other Newspaper Stories, and a school paper tells it about an unnamed editor. It was first pinned on Charles A. Dana in 1902, after his death in 1897. Quote Investigator ↗ finds no solid evidence that Dana or any other named editor coined it.

source.excerpt: “You’ll soon assimilate the idea. Now, for instance, ‘A dog bites a man’—that’s a story; ‘A man bites a dog’—that’s a good story,” etc.
trail: 1899: A fictional old reporter in Jesse Lynch Williams’s The Stolen Story says “‘A dog bites a man’—that’s a story; ‘A man bites a dog’—that’s a good story.” (1899 scan ↗)
February 1899: An Indianapolis school paper tells of Richard Harding Davis asking “an editor” what news is, and gives a man-bites-dog answer. No editor is named. (Barry Popik ↗)

1902: The line is credited to “the great Dana” in The Inlander (June). The Omaha Daily Bee (August 3) reprints a Buffalo Commercial item in which Davis puts the question to Dana himself. (Quote Investigator ↗)
1918: Frank M. O’Brien’s The Story of the Sun gives the line to Sun city editor John B. Bogart: “When a dog bites a man, that is not news, because it happens so often.” (1918 scan ↗)
source.excerptNote: No author is named for the maxim itself. Quote Investigator thinks Williams was probably repeating a saying already going around newsrooms, not making it up. The popular two-sentence wording on this page is a later, tidier form.

author.name: Charles A. Dana
author.kicker: The name the saying attached to
author.heading: About the editor it’s pinned on
author.metaLine: 1819–1897 · Editor of The New York Sun
author.bio: Charles Anderson Dana was Horace Greeley’s managing editor at the New-York Tribune and served as Assistant Secretary of War during the Civil War. In 1868 he became editor and part-owner of The New York Sun, whose brisk, story-driven news style made it famous among reporters. That reputation probably explains why a newsroom maxim about what counts as news attached itself to his name after he died.

misattribution.heading: Why so many editors get the credit
misattribution.intro: Over the decades the same maxim has been hung on at least six newspapermen. Quote Investigator ↗ finds that each credit appears late or second-hand.

items.why: He is the earliest named source, but the credits start in 1902 items, after his death in 1897. Earlier versions name no one, and none comes from his own writings. (QI ↗)

Frank M. O’Brien’s 1918 The Story of the Sun credits the Sun city editor, describing him as one “who absorbed the Dana idea of news.” That is the source behind Bogart entries in modern quotation books. (1918 scan ↗)
Arthur Brisbane named Cummings, another Sun man, in a 1921 column. Back in 1912 Brisbane had used the same line without naming anyone. (QI ↗)
A 1909 Denver Post editorial put the words in Greeley’s mouth. QI rates this as late and second-hand. (QI ↗)
A 1922 Boston Globe column said a London journalist had heard Northcliffe give a definition of news that was “nothing but the familiar saying” credited to various American editors. (QI ↗)
By 1934 a Georgia paper noted that the saying had been credited to both Pulitzer and Northcliffe. (QI ↗)

misattribution.truthLine: The maxim was in print by 1899 with no author named. The earliest credits to Dana that researchers have found date from 1902, after his death in 1897. Quote Investigator concludes that the evidence for every named candidate is weak. (Quote Investigator ↗)

context.heading: How an anonymous anecdote got a famous name
lead: In the earliest versions, the man-bites-dog definition of news is an anecdote with no name attached. In the February 1899 school-paper telling that Barry Popik ↗ records, a young Richard Harding Davis puts the question to “an editor.” By August 1902 the Omaha Daily Bee was telling the same Davis story with Charles A. Dana as the editor who answered.

That is the usual path for a newsroom joke: it fastens onto the most famous editor associated with the paper it is told about. O’Brien’s 1918 history of the Sun gave it to city editor John B. Bogart instead, and later writers spread the credit to Cummings, Greeley, Northcliffe and Pulitzer.
context.detailsSummary: What O’Brien offered as Dana’s own definition of news
detailsBody: Straight after the Bogart anecdote, O’Brien’s The Story of the Sun ↗ prints what it calls “Mr. Dana’s own definition of news.” The passage defines news as “everything that occurs, everything which is of human interest” and closes: “whatever the divine Providence permitted to occur I was not too proud to report.” It contains no dog.
context.pull: “The Sun always waited for the man to bite the dog.” — Frank M. O’Brien, 1918
